implementation_notes: Go has no authorization in the standard library; the local idiom replaces the Policy/Guard class pair with a small interface and a wrapper function. The policy is a value implementing Authorize(ctx context.Context, sub Subject, act Action, res Resource) error (or a plain function of the same shape), the guard is an http.Handler middleware or a method-level wrapper that calls it before delegating, and the request-scoped security context travels in context.Context values set by the authentication middleware. What replaces the classic structure: interface satisfaction and handler wrapping replace inheritance and virtual dispatch; return typed errors (errors.Is(err, ErrDenied)) so the guard maps denial to 403 consistently. The explicit OO form is still justified only when subject or resource types have several implementations that carry their own rule data.
pitfalls: A middleware guards only the routes it wraps; handlers mounted elsewhere (gRPC methods, background workers) reaching the same resource need their own guard call.
Sharing a mutable policy value across goroutines without synchronisation races; rebuilding it per request instead avoids races but churns allocations.
Context values are loosely typed: define an unexported key type and verify the subject exists - a missing subject must deny, not panic or default to anonymous-with-rights.
